beginner.headline: Protein Powder Prices Go Up
beginner.brief: Amarpreet has been drinking protein shakes for many years. His protein shakes are now much more expensive. In 2020, his protein cost about £60. Last year, the price went up to £120. More people want protein, but there is not enough. So, the cost of ingredients is higher. Amarpreet will buy a cheaper brand now. Evie will not buy protein powder anymore.

intermediate.headline: Protein Prices Soar: Consumers Feel the Squeeze
intermediate.brief: Consumers are feeling the pinch from the rising cost of protein. Amarpreet Singh has been drinking protein shakes since he was 16. Amarpreet says a 4.5kg bag of the whey protein he buys cost around £60 in 2020. By last year, its price had gone up to £120. Fourteen years later, shakes are still part of his routine, but they have become considerably more expensive. Over the years, protein powders and shakes have attracted a much broader customer base. Evie Lewis began using protein powder because she felt she wasn't getting enough protein in her diet. At £32.99 for a 420g tub, Evie is feeling the high price. She admits, "I've been rationing it and using less than what's suggested." The growing appetite for protein is running up against a problem: supply has not kept pace. Manufacturers say that increasing production takes time and is costly, as producing high-protein whey requires specialist processing and drying equipment. Some companies are starting to adapt what they make by changing recipes or looking for cheaper sources of protein. For students like Evie, managing on a much tighter budget, buying protein is a different story. She says that now she is at university, protein is not a necessity right now. One protein user explains, "If you're doing exercise and not taking any, you feel like you wouldn't be recovering properly."

advanced.headline: Protein Users Squeezed as Costs Soar: The Rise of 'Proteinflation'
advanced.brief: Consumers are experiencing significant financial pressure due to the escalating cost of protein supplements. Amarpreet Singh, who has consumed protein shakes since age 16, has witnessed a substantial increase in prices over fourteen years. A 4.5kg bag of whey protein he purchased for around £60 in 2020 had soared to £120 by last year, though he secured one for less via eBay. Among his gym peers, this upward trend in protein costs has colloquially been termed "proteinflation." Over recent years, protein powders have attracted a considerably wider demographic, with food manufacturers diversifying into high-protein versions of various everyday items. Nineteen-year-old student Evie Lewis recently started using protein powder as she believed her diet lacked sufficient protein. She finds the £32.99 price for a 420g tub prohibitive, leading her to conserve the product by using less than the recommended amount. Max Longman, a long-term user, notes his monthly expenditure on whey protein has climbed from approximately £45 to £60 within the last year. The burgeoning demand for protein is exacerbated by new weight-loss drugs, whose users are often advised to maintain adequate protein intake to preserve muscle mass. This surging appetite, however, is encountering a significant obstacle: supply has not grown sufficiently to meet the heightened consumption. Consequently, wholesale prices for crucial ingredients have sharply escalated, intensifying the pressure on consumers. For instance, the European wholesale price of a common high-protein whey type was 130% higher in late August compared to the previous year, and more than four times its value three years ago. Manufacturers acknowledge that increasing production is both time-consuming and capital-intensive, particularly as high-protein whey processing demands specialized equipment. Some companies, like UK sports nutrition firm Warrior, are exploring alternative protein sources to mitigate production costs. Kieran Fisher, Warrior's founder, indicated that their whey protein powder's shelf price rose from £12.50 to £17.99, yet the company still subsidises it. While wholesale prices for high-protein whey have stabilised recently, they remain substantially elevated compared to several years prior. Despite these increases, committed users like Max view protein as increasingly vital for post-exercise recovery, making it a widespread staple. Conversely, students like Evie, operating on stringent budgets, are less inclined to continue purchasing it, deeming it a dispensable item for now. Amarpreet considers continued protein consumption a luxury and is seeking a more affordable brand, though he expects to pay around £100 per bag.
